Marking October 27 under the theme 'Your Window to the World', UNESCO's Memory of the World Programme is partnering with Japan to restore and digitize imperiled African broadcasting collections.

The Bright Side:
Rescuing vulnerable analogue recordings from decay and conflict ensures that ordinary voices, local music, and cultural struggles remain permanently accessible to future generations rather than lost to silence.

Social Physics Analysis:
This project demonstrates genuine altruistic stewardship. Rather than hoarding historical assets or manufacturing scarcity, institutions coordinate open technical capacity, solving the physical decay of irreplaceable archives.

With stated goals translating directly into physical preservation within 0.03 units of divergence, the process anchors firmly in systemic realization.

The Unavoidable Truth: Fragile magnetic tape naturally degrades without urgent physical restoration and digitization.

The Unavoidable Lie: Cultural history can survive neglect and climate disasters without dedicated funding.

Institutional memory is the substrate of collective identity. Converting fragile magnetic physical media into accessible digital records protects human history from the thermodynamic certainty of decay.

Hearing everyday songs, local stories, and voices from decades ago saved from oblivion is profoundly moving. Every restored tape is a lost voice coming home to future generations.

Old school magnetic cassettes rotting in storage boxes is a tragedy waiting to happen. Huge respect to the audio geeks in Mogadishu and Zambia pulling 45,000 classics back from the brink.

World Day for Audiovisual Heritage: Protecting memory at risk

Actual Article Body:
UNESCO

UNESCO

News

The theme of this year’s Day, “Your Window to the World”, recognizes the impact that audiovisual heritage has on establishing shared understanding between cultures across the globe.

In 2026, the UNESCO Memory of the World Programme implemented several projects in relation to endangered documentary heritage, including in its audiovisual form. With the support of the Japanese Funds-In-Trust and Japan’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, the project on Preservation and Accessibility of Documentary Heritage has been focusing on policy advocacy and capacity-building for specialists working in memory institutions.

Among these projects are efforts to preserve and digitize approximately 45,000 analogue tape recordings held by Radio Mogadishu. This work demonstrates the great value of audiovisual archives for the country’s history and identity. People’s everyday stories, local news, political speeches, entertainment programmes, and music – all of them form part of Somalia’s cultural DNA, and need to be preserved and passed on to future generations.

A distinct Initiative to Safeguard Documentary Heritage at Risk is a series of projects that aim to protect documentary heritage that can become permanently damaged or disappear due to natural disasters and man-made threats.

In Zambia, the National Broadcasting Corporation (ZNBC) holds collections of audiovisual materials documenting significant periods of Southern Africa’s history. However, the consequences of natural disasters, unfavorable storage conditions, and outdated formats underlined the urgent need to save records from permanent loss.

UNESCO is helping ensure the survival of these archives through several restoration and digitization techniques. This includes identifying and prioritizing at-risk analogue tapes and film holdings, while ensuring their long-term preservation through migration to formats that remain compatible with evolving technologies.

The UNESCO website dedicated to the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage 2026 will showcase events taking place around the world in relation to the celebration, shared by both UNESCO Field Offices and the Coordinating Council of Audiovisual Archives Associations (CCAAA).

The MoW Programme was established in 1992 to safeguard documentary heritage for present and future generations. Guided by the 2015 UNESCO Recommendation on the Preservation of, and Access to, Documentary Heritage Including in Digital Form, the Programme facilitates the preservation and accessibility of these vital records, while raising public awareness of their value. Its innovative digital tools further enhance accessibility, bringing history to life in engaging and meaningful ways.

UNESCO applies a zero tolerance policy against all forms of harassment.
